senses: A beautiful young man, like the mythological Greek Narcissus
ety: Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos), ultimately either from Pre-Greek or related to νάρκη (nárkē).

senses: An act of taking a small, quick bite, or several of such bites, especially with the front teeth; the bite or bites so taken.
A light bite of a person or animal, or part of their body, especially one which is loving or playful; a nip.
An amount of food that is or can be taken into the mouth through a small bite; a small mouthful.
A slight show of interest in something, such as a commercial opportunity or a proposal.
ety: The verb is derived from Late Middle English nebillen, nebyll (“to peck away at (something), nibble; (figurative) to attempt to sing (a part of a song)”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Middle Low German nibbelen (“to eat in small bites, peck”) (modern German Low German nibbeln, gnibbeln, knibbeln), possibly a variant of knabbelen, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press”) or imitative. The noun is derived from the verb. Cognates * Middle Dutch cnibbelen (modern Dutch knibbelen (“to gnaw; to murmur”), nibbelen (“to nibble”)) * Saterland Frisian nibje (“to nibble”) * W

senses: Having tusks, especially prominent tusks.
ety: From Middle English tusky, equivalent to tusk + -y.

senses: A caramel-coloured flavoured bitters made from oranges, gentian, and quinquina, traditionally accompanying beer in the east and north of France.
ety: Borrowed from French picon, named after inventor Gaétan Picon (1809–1882).

senses: Any of a family of alloys with a zinc base and alloying elements of aluminium, magnesium, and copper.
ety: From a trademark. It is an acronym of the German names for the metals: Zink, Aluminium, Magnesium, Kupfer.

senses: The process leading to the formation or deposition of layers, especially of sedimentary rocks.
A layering of musical texture.
Society's categorization of people into socioeconomic strata.
The process of treating seeds to simulate natural conditions that the seeds must experience before germination can occur, often involving exposure to cold.
A classification or arrangement of things into different categories or groups.
The ability to be completely determined in a definite way; the quality of being determinate.
Something with which to stroke.

A principal, low-level cloud type in the form of a gray layer with a rather uniform base, usually not associated with precipitation, and capable of producing corona phenomena and a weak, uniform luminance.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin strātus (“spread or stretched out”). Coined by the British chemist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard (1772–1864): see the 1803 quotation. Doublet of strath.

senses: A fabric filter; an air pollution control device that removes particulates out of air or gas released from commercial processes or combustion for electricity generation.
Synonym of juice box.
ety: Genericized trademark of Popper (“a brand name”), an Australian juice brand owned by Queensland United Foods. First attested in 1978.

senses: of, related to, or derived from silica
ety: From Latin silex, silicis (“a flint”). Compare French silicique.

senses: A drug used for its effect on the immune system.
Having a branched cluster of flowers.
ety: From panicle, a compound inflorescence in which the flowers are arranged along a single central axis.

senses: Any of a class of strong, heat-resistant synthetic fibres, used in aerospace and military applications.
A district in Indonesia.
examples: However,rather than a central fund for which communities compete through project proposals, the project allocates block grants of about $43,000–$125,000 a year directly to all participating kecamatans and villages.

senses: Such trees themselves, particularly the Chinese cinnamon, Cinnamomum cassia.
The sweet osmanthus (O. fragrans).
ety: From Latin cassia (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek κασσία, κασία, κάσια (kassía, kasía, kásia), from Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), from Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”). Compare Kezia.

senses: Any small structure shaped like a cup, such as at the base of an acorn, or the sucker on the feet of some flies.
ety: From cup + -ule.; former is derived from Old English copp of Germanic origin thus not related (false cognate) to cupula of Latin origin, but perhaps influenced it
examples: Then they extract a three-angled beechnut from its cupule, weigh it, and push it into the loam.

senses: A double-headed serpent in Inca and other Andean mythology.
A person who manages, or works in, a warehouse.
A fleuron depicting an ivy leaf.
ety: From the genus name Hedera, in turn from Latin hedera (“ivy”).

senses: The fruit of this tree; the macadamia nut.
ety: From the genus name Macadamia, coined by the German-Australian botanist Ferdinand von Mueller in 1857, in honor of John Macadam, whose surname is an alternative spelling of MacAdam, from Scottish Gaelic Mac Àdhaimh (“Adam's son”). By surface analysis, Mac- + Adam + -ia.

senses: Resembling a tongue.
Having a particular manner of speaking.
Having a tongue for towing.
ety: From Middle English tonged, tunged, equivalent to tongue + -ed. Compare Old English ġetynġe (“skilled with speech, talkative, eloquent”).

senses: An Internet user, particularly a Usenet user.
ety: From net + -ie, on the model of Trekkie.
examples: Any nettie ever driven in Los Angeles?
The dissemination of information through this newsgroup is substantial, but most netties do not subscribe to alt.drugs, and they make up only a small fraction of the general public.

senses: A long, narrow-fronted hall or vaulted portal found in Levantine homes, often open to the outside.
A fortnight in a month of the Hindu lunar calendar.
Using two eyes or viewpoints; especially, using two eyes or viewpoints to ascertain distance.
The quality of being impulsive, impulsiveness; inclination to act on impulse rather than thought.
A powdered form of polyvinylpyrrolidone that is used as a dispersing and suspending agent in drugs.
To make or become a foe.
To treat or behave as a foe; be hostile towards.
ety: From be- + foe, modelled after befriend.
examples: Take it from me; it is helpful to remain buoyant when identifying fish to befriend or "befoe."

What will the great coming Russian revolution do? Will it destroy the aristocracy, as in France, or will it leave it standing? Will it befriend or befoe the large non-Russian element of the western provinces?
M. C. Witherspoon in the presence of each other Witnessed the due execution thereof. J. J. McMullan Sworn to befoe me this 21st day of Jan. 1842.

senses: The leader of a župa, or administrative unit, among various South Slavic peoples.
ety: Of Slavic origin, from Proto-Slavic *županъ, from *župa (“area, district”).

senses: A social hierarchy in which the mediocre prevails.
A traditional Japanese form of storytelling using picture scrolls, revived in the twentieth century by travelling showmen.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 紙芝居 (literally “paper drama”).
examples: Japan Society will honor it with kamishibai, a traditional form of puppet theater.

senses: Something which is added or summed.
Having tassels.
examples: Even the mantelpiece is adorned with a totally unfunctional tasselled valance rather like an altar frontal.

senses: An animal raised for its wool, especially an angora rabbit.
Someone who works with wool.
examples: With a cost of $1.00 to $2.00 per rabbit for feed, the profit should be at or near $5.00 per rabbit from good woolers which produce approximately one pound of wool each per year.
The breeder who sells the rabbits at a very early age could very well be selling excellent woolers or possibly only average producers, only time will tell.
He was fined another twenty pounds for usury after charging a local wooler — a Protestant — twenty pounds for a short-term hundred-pound loan.

senses: The act of reciprocating; interchange of acts; a mutual giving and returning.
Alternate recurrence or action; as, the reciprocation of the sea in the flow and ebb of tides, or the back and forth motion in a piston engine.
A traditional village.
A district or suburb where a former village once stood.
ety: Borrowed from Malay kampung (“enclosure; quarter of a town occupied by a certain nationality; village”). Doublet of kampang. Cognates * Dutch kampoeng

senses: A gender-neutral term of affection.
To serve a writ of this kind upon.
